#120919. Tech Report: Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

Tech Report: Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota is getting into electric bikes.
  • The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.
  • And when Toyota notes compact, it means it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

And when Toyota notes compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the firm is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

In a recent development, toyota calls the fresh Scion a “freedom lab” where the company can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota indicated its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

Recent findings suggest that and I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota claims the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

It has been revealed that toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota states his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t announced production plans or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota notes a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

According to recent reports, I’m obviously a massive believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

Recent findings suggest that but hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Red Bull Formula 1 team has a brutal reputation for chewing up promising upcoming drivers, but Kiwi driver Liam Lawson has kept his focus after being demoted from being Max Verstappen’s teammate back to the junior Visa Cash App Racing Bulls (VCARB) team in 2025. Lawson had an excellent year with the Racing Bulls so far, including a top-10 finish and a respectable stand-in back at Red Bull over the summer filling in for an injured Isack Hadjar.

Despite his performance, he was unsure of his seat for 2027 until just a few days ago, when VCARB confirmed Lawson and teammate Arvid Lindblad will both return for next year. Discussion of the future was still off limits for this interview, but it was a noticeably relaxed Liam Lawson who sat down with us to talk about significant trucks, sad songs, and what makes Vegas such a tough race.

Car and Driver: What is the week leading up to a race like, especially a media-heavy one like Las Vegas?

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

Liam Lawson: Vegas is a unique race in many aspects. The timings of it [Vegas is a night race]. And then this weekend for us, this year in general with these cars, there were upcoming regulations, new power units. Every weekend has been a bit of a challenge to learn. Vegas is very cold and not high grip, it's very, very low grip. The track’s quite dirty as well. They open the street up at night and it sort of makes it quite difficult for us when we come back the next day. So the prep that goes in is a little bit more than normal. We’re definitely doing a lot on the simulator side.

Do you guys have a way to do simulator work on the road, not just sort of between races?

Recent findings suggest that oh, no, unfortunately not. It’s back at base Milton Keynes. So for a triple header like this [Vegas, Qatar, Abu Dhabi], we will do time on all three tracks before and get them basically dialed and then go to the races, but we don’t have time to go back in between races, unfortunately.

I guess I hadn’t really thought of it that way, but because the setup is so different, even tracks that you’re very familiar with are going to be almost like new tracks. Like each race you’re all running for the first time with this setup.

Yeah, it’s very different, especially at the start of the year. I would say things are now getting a lot more consistent as we get in the groove of things. It's been tricky and we’ve just been learning through the year and the cars have been getting a lot better as well as we bring upgrades. It’s been a lot busier. We started probably in January, a lot earlier than normal with preseason testing and trying to get a handle on these cars.

According to recent reports, you’re known as a pretty technical guy, a pretty technical driver. What’s your relationship with your team in terms of giving them feedback on the cars or being involved in setup?

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147.

In a recent development, it’s very different depending on driver. I think it’s key the relationship you have with your engineers, that they understand the type of driver that you are as well, because, the way that you give feedback sometimes can be misheard, you know, or like misunderstood. My relationship with the guys I work with has strengthened a lot through the year. Alex [race engineer Alexandre Iliopoulos], when I’m speaking about something, he knows pretty much what I’m saying and understands it.

Recent findings suggest that every driver is different. I would definitely say I’m more invested on the technical side as well, especially on the development side of the car. And the direction that we’ve been going in through the year where we’ve been trying to improve the car-specific areas. I’ve been a little bit lucky as well that I got to drive a couple of different cars as well in the past and obviously this year as well.

What’s the feedback process after a session?

It’s something that is different for everybody, but when we come in from a session, we basically sit in a major circle and the specific roles on the team go through their individual feedback on the session. I talk about what I feel in the car and report that back. And then I talk about the main things that I need from the car to be quicker in the next sessions.

You sound very comfortable with that. Another key part of your guys’ job, especially in the last few years as F1 has become so much more mainstream, is social media. How do you like that kind of stuff? How do you deal with it? Do you think it’s fun? Do you hate it?

Probably somewhere in the middle, I would say. I don’t mind it sometimes, as long as it’s not in the way of performance. That’s what we’re all focused on. But it’s been good. I mean, the sport is in a great place and the support we have as drivers now is growing every year. We see that at all the races we go to, especially in the U.S. It’s been incredible to see. Very cool. So it’s mostly positive. And some of it can be quite fun to do.

Do you like the ones where they hit you with quiz questions? Or do you want to do little dance moves? What’s your favorite kind of social post?

According to recent reports, [laughs] Definitely not doing little dance moves. The sort of question games that I’ll sit down with Arvid and do are good. The ones that take the least amount of time, they’re probably the ones that I enjoy doing the most on a race weekend. But we’ve done some cool stuff outside of track as well, and at some recent races with the team like doing a [musical] performance recently in Austin.

In a recent development, oh let’s talk about that! You’re a musician as well as a driver.

In a recent development, guitar. That’s something I’ve done since I was very young. My parents had me playing and learning classical guitar. Now I just play for fun, mostly like country music.

Industry observers note that there’s a fair amount of you guys who play instruments. Could you put an all-F1 band together? Doesn’t Charles play piano?

Yeah, Lewis is very good as well.

In a recent development, I have no idea. I don’t think anybody plays drums. It’s either guitar or piano but I would say most of the grid is not musically gifted.

Back to cars. Is there any street car that you really like to drive?

In a recent development, yeah, and it’s really only in the U.S. I get to drive it just ’cause it’s so significant that it doesn’t fit in Europe or anywhere else in the world. At the moment I drive a Ford Raptor R. I drove here today from California, from Newport Beach. It’s the ultimate daily. It’s kind of got everything. It’s very high horsepower. It’s got basically Trophy Truck suspension, and it’s comfortable as well. It’s just not very good on fuel, so it’s definitely expensive to fill up during the day.

In a recent development, what, they don’t give you a fuel card at Visa Cash App, Liam? Next time you do that drive, you can actually drive from Los Angeles to Las Vegas pretty much all off-road.

It has been revealed that what? Really? I’d be very interested to do that because that’s like what this truck is made for.

Any other hobbies besides jumping Raptors and playing country music?

According to recent reports, I ride dirt bikes. I’ve got a track that I built in Latest Zealand at home. I have a KTM 250. It’s probably not something the team loves.

Yeah, mostly motocross. The track I have at home, it’s not too crazy. It’s on the safer side, you know, I would say it doesn’t have any like crazy doubles or stuff.

Are you telling me that or are you telling your manager in the background?

Okay, last question, what’s your favorite country music song?

“Whiskey Glasses,” Morgan Wallen.

How a red wolf gets a checkup

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, annual human checkups are relatively straightforward.
  • We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam.
  • “The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, annual human checkups are relatively straightforward. You hop onto the exam table, stick your tongue out, stare straight ahead as the doctor beams light into your eyes, let them tap their small hammer against that wildly uncomfortable spot under your kneecap, etc. But for wildlife, it’s a whole other experience.

We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam. But what about another favorite carnivore—wolves? According to Vicki Scharfberg, from Roger Williams Park Zoo & Carousel Village in Rhode Island, the annual wellness examination for red wolves (Canis rufus) is not that different from a pet dog’s annual veterinary visit.

“The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.

In a recent development, the checkup includes a physical examination at the wolf enclosure or the zoo veterinary hospital, bloodwork, vaccinations, heartworm prevention care, and if necessary, parasite treatment. A social media post by Roger Williams Park Zoo showcases their red wolf named Frye thoroughly knocked out on the exam table, undergoing an oral exam, among other things.

Industry observers note that the team uses the bloodwork to check on the wolf’s organs and screen for heartworm disease. Interestingly, their vaccines are the exact same ones veterinarians give to domestic dogs for rabies, distemper, parvovirus, and leptospirosis.

Industry observers note that heartworm prevention treatment involves a long-acting 12 month injection. Heartworm disease is caused by grossly long worms called heartworms that take up residence in an animals’ heart, lungs, and related blood vessels. This parasitic condition triggers severe lung disease, heart failure, and damages other organs. Heartworm is potentially fatal, and in addition to wolves can also impact animals including dogs, cats, ferrets, foxes, and humans.

“If something abnormal is found on the examination, we follow up with additional diagnostics like x-rays, ultrasound, or a consult with a veterinary specialist (dentist, cardiologist, etc),” Scharfberg concludes.

F1 and Manufacturers Unanimously Agree to a Initiative to Return to V8 Engines in 2030

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FIA began the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend by announcing that all manufacturers have agreed to the framework to bring turbocharged V8 engines back to F1 and move away from the current V6 turbo.
  • This move has long been expected, with hopes that it will make engine building easier and cheaper while bringing back the sound that motorsport fans deeply miss.
  • The sound of the V8 engines was a rally cry for fans and has been sorely missed by audiences worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FIA began the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend by announcing that all manufacturers have agreed to the framework to bring turbocharged V8 engines back to F1 and move away from the current V6 turbo.

This move has long been expected, with hopes that it will make engine building easier and cheaper while bringing back the sound that motorsport fans deeply miss.

The sound of the V8 engines was a rally cry for fans and has been sorely missed by audiences worldwide.

The F1 engine manufacturers agreed to a rough-out overarching proposal to move to a 2.1-liter turbocharged V8 from 2030 onwards, with a lower charge of electrical power reducing the hybrid output from 350kW to 200kW, a decrease of nearly 56 percent.

The FIA unveiled that ‘The initiative is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and placing greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing.”.

With everyone in agreement, PU manufacturers will start to jockey between improving the latest car entering a sophomore season of new regulations and game planning for the major change coming just three seasons down the line.

It’s been 13 years since manufacturers last built a V8 engine for F1.

“This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1,” FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem stated. “From the outset, I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

Industry observers note that “The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”.

Victoria Beaver is a nomadic sports writer who spends her time hopping between race tracks and hippie farms. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hyundai absolutely knocked the teasers for then Hyundai N Vision 74 out of the park. I mean, a hydrogen-electric hybrid that's an actual sports car, with all the style of a 1970s wedge car? The internet loved the idea. But, unfortunately, that's probably what the N Vision will remain—an idea. The aims for production are on ice.

Sources indicate that simon Loasby, the head of Hyundai's Design Center, explained toThe Drive that the decision came down to business. When the South Korean automaker simply couldn't justify the business case for the car, it decided to not move forward with production in the foreseeable future. Here's what Loasby told the publication when asked if the automaker planned to make a production version of the N Vision 74:.

At the moment, no. We were really on it. We had the production clay model of it and the exterior, interior, and so on.

Industry observers note that it comes down to the maths of how you judge what the business case is. And that if you’re very tight with the business case on only that car, the volumes of that car and the impact, you got no chance.

If you open it to the overall brand-raising profile value of that, you have a bigger chance. But as yet, [no].

Recent findings suggest that many of you reading this are likely part car lover and part EV enthusiast. Me too, which is why I'm immensely disappointed that Hyundai decided to cancel prepares to build this awesome concept.

It has been revealed that after all, EVs are damn fun. Instant torque, low center of gravity. It's pretty much everything that an an enthusiast wants out of a sports car—even if EVs inherently are a bit heavier and lack a row-your-own gearbox. It also used the beloved Stinger as a base to build the car. But rather than the 3.3-liter twin-turbocharged V6, Hyundai stuffed it with the Nexo's hydrogen fuel cells and two electric motors.

That mentioned, not all has gone to waste.

One of the coolest parts of the coupe was its retro styling. That was inspired by the original Hyundai Pony coupe, which was designed by the legendary Giorgetto Giugiaro (the same guy who designed the VW Golf, DeLorean DMC-12, and a plethora of other icons).

In a recent development, loasby claims that Hyundai's head of design, SangYup Lee, convinced the tech giant not to throw away the design work from the N Vision concept. Instead, it reused some of the design elements for upcoming models like the all new 2027 Hyundai Elantra.

"[T]hat top view as you notice, even in the pillar and side view up to the roof crease and the flatness of the roof, that’s all playbook N74," he told The Drive. He later hinted more could be coming: “Just imagine what an N version of [Elantra] can be. It’s really good, it’s awesome.”.

Maybe it was the idea of using hydrogen that killed the N Vision concept. Or perhaps that coupes have seem to go the way of the dodo in recent years. Whatever the reason, it's just unfortunate for enthusiasts who were pumped to see a sport-tuned FCEV in the distance.

According to recent reports, one glimmer of hope is that Loasby didn't say that the car is dead forever. Just that Hyundai couldn't make a business case for it "at the moment." Perhaps we might get something with two-doors, a striking design, and battery power in the future. Until then, I'm staying pumped about the Rivian R3X.

You’ll be able to pick from Alice, Soldier 0 – Anby, or Astra. Zhao will herself be available as a login bonus alongside 1,000 Polychromes, a newly introduced outfit for Jane, and more. Breaking: Tesla Cybertruck’s already impressive turning radius gets even tighter

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.
  • Recent findings suggest that but there’s a catch.
  • Sources indicate that tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out an update that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

Recent findings suggest that but there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla plans to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

Sources indicate that tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to new Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla mentioned the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”.

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to fresh Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0.

Tesla didn’t share a new turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

The Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

Even before this revision, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

Recent findings suggest that and Tesla always noted there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software upgrade would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the organization had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”.

Tesla hasn’t stated whether this enhancement delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

Credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice revision.

But it’s hard to get excited about it.

According to recent reports, and 39.4 feet turning circle for the Cadillac Escalade which also has rear wheel steering. As does the iX5 (39.7'), MB GLC (36.7') and EQS (35.8'), the Lucid Gravity (38.4), Hummer 37.4', Cayenne (38.4) and a around two dozen other vehicles on the market today. So maybe this is not such major news after all?

Earlier this month, Musk confirmed that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

Recent findings suggest that so Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

It’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

#120911. Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • It has been revealed that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

That brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

It has been revealed that many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

Recent findings suggest that there’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks shows that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

So bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

“They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

Which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

You might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

There’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

Squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

In a recent development, they are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University demonstrated this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

Sources indicate that the results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

Sources indicate that other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

#120910. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker.
  • Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand.
  • This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”.

Industry observers note that the game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Sources indicate that stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

It has been revealed that boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research fresh mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Avancier debuts Honda’s new two-motor hybrid powertrain, called Honda Hybrid.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda has revealed the second-generation Avancier today, and while it won’t be offered in the United States, the newly introduced SUV gives us a preview of the upcoming next-generation CR-V and other hybrid models due out over the next few years. Designed for Asian markets such as Thailand, Japan, and China, the three-row Avancier sits above the CR-V and pairs clean, modern styling with a new hybrid powertrain.

The Avancier debuts Honda’s new two-motor hybrid powertrain, called Honda Hybrid. For now, Honda is remaining tight-lipped about many of the details. The automaker promises “excellent fuel economy,” and the Avancier also releases Honda’s new DualPower eAWD system, controlling the front and rear wheels independently via separate electric motors. The S+ Shift function, which simulates gearshifts for the hybrid powertrain and has been seen on the Civic Hybrid and Prelude, is also present.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 33101.

The Avancier is also the first Honda that is not an EV to feature the brand’s latest “H” logo, which was introduced in 2024 and was originally set to be used exclusively for electric models. With Honda cancelling its trio of EVs that were meant to be built in Ohio—the Acura RSX and Honda 0-Series Saloon and 0-Series SUV—the manufacturer has decided to roll out the simplified “H” logo across its entire lineup starting in 2027.

According to recent reports, the new badge sits proudly on the nose of the Avancier, just below a thin opening that connects the squinting LED daytime running lights. The main headlights sit below, linked by a series of geometric trim pieces that, along with a vent in the lower bumper, help channel air to the engine.

The side profile of the Avancier is clean, with flush door handles and gloss black trim that frames the wheel arches and the bottom of the SUV. Around back, the taillights consist of blocky, vertical elements connected by a light bar. While we don’t think the next CR-V will look exactly like the Avancier, we expect to see elements such as the thin DRLs to migrate across the Honda lineup in the coming years.

The cabin will also likely inform future U.S.-bound Hondas, and it gives off an airy, tranquil vibe. Unfortunately, the Avancier appears to have skipped out on most physical controls, putting nearly every function into the sizable screen that sits above the air vents in the center of the dashboard. We hope Honda reconsiders this approach in the U.S., given how much we appreciate the intuitive, straightforward physical buttons and knobs found in current Hondas.

See all results for used Honda for sale near 33101.

The Avancier also introduces a column-mounted shifter, a feature we also tested on a next-generation Civic prototype we drove last year. It frees up space on the center console. The steering wheel has an unusual squared-off shape with a flat bottom, and behind it there is a digital gauge cluster. Glowing ambient lighting and white upholstery create a futuristic, sterile appearance, and a panoramic glass roof extends all the way to the third row.

Recent findings suggest that honda loaded the SUV with premium features, such as heated and ventilated seats in the second row and a 12-speaker Bose stereo with Dolby Atmos. There’s also a system that uses cameras on the inside and outside of the Avancier to let owners check on the cabin and car’s surroundings remotely via a smartphone app.

It has been revealed that while the Avancier won’t be sold on our shores, we expect to see elements of its styling on upcoming Hondas, as well as its upcoming hybrid powertrain. Honda aims to launch 15 new hybrid models globally by 2030, which includes a new CR-V next year, as well as a new Civic and a heavily updated Accord in the near future.

  • Those components combine to create a massive 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour, an increase of 72 percent over the 296 GTB that won Road & Track Performance Car of the Year in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the new-for-2026 Ferrari 296 Speciale is a sharper, faster, and more track-oriented variant of the brand’s V-6 supercar—but that doesn’t mean it is the only high-performance variant of the car that Ferrari will build. In a somewhat surprising break from recent tradition, Ferrari is also going to make a Challenge Stradale variant of the 296 to sell alongside the Speciale.

As the name suggests, the Challenge Stradale is a road-going variant of the 296 that shares a lot in common with the race car currently used in various Ferrari Challenge series. Specifically, its aerodynamic elements are strikingly similar to the new 296 Challenge Evo, which was revealed alongside the new road car on November 21. The massive rear wing, front dive planes, and aggressive rear splitter are all extremely similar to design elements seen on that race car.

Those components combine to create a massive 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour, an increase of 72 percent over the 296 GTB that won Road & Track Performance Car of the Year in 2024. Downforce is also up 401 lbs at that speed on the 296 Speciale, an increase of 29 percent.

The removal of the hybrid system means a reduction in power, dropping from a combined system output of 819 horsepower in the 296 GTB to an engine-only output of 670 hp in the Challenge Stradale. The simplified powertrain and stripped out interior mean serious reductions in weight to match, though; the Challenge Stradale is 309 lbs lighter than the GTB and 176 lbs lighter than the Speciale.

Does the reduction in weight and increase in downforce make the 296 Challenge Stradale faster than the hybrid 296 Speciale already on the market? Not necessarily. Ferrari claims the Challenge Stradale is half a second a lap faster at its Fiorano test track, but marginally slower at a high-speed circuit like Monza. The more powerful Speciale should be quicker on other tracks with the on-throttle time necessary to allow the hybrid to stretch its legs, while the lighter Challenge Stradale should have the advantage on more technical circuits with more off-throttle time.

According to recent reports, the other major differentiation between the Speciale and the Challenge Stradale is availability. While that other high-end 296 variant was a limited-run model, Ferrari stresses that the Challenge Stradale is a part of its regular lineup, and should be more available to buyers. It remains a Ferrari, so the market is unlikely to be flooded with 296s with massive wings in the years to come, but by supercar standards, it should be relatively attainable.

According to recent reports, ferrari has not yet unveiled a price for the American market, but the brand states that it should start at the equivalent of just under $320,000 in Italy, including value-added tax. Prices in one region do not necessarily translate directly to another, but that number would leave the 296 Challenge Stradale in the general range of the similarly track-focused likes of Porsche’s 911 GT3 RS and Ford’s Mustang GTD.

How much does charging an EV really cost? This Redditor claims $7 per month

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most common questions asked by first-time EV buyers is about the cost of electricity.
  • According to recent reports, whether we’re talking gasoline, diesel, or electricity, one driver’s fuel costs can look dramatically different from another’s.
  • “My wife and I recently retired and moved from a car dependent, rural/suburban area to a large, walkable city with good light rail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most common questions asked by first-time EV buyers is about the cost of electricity. Whether they plan to charge at home or find charging in the wild, everyone wants to know what to expect when it comes time to top off their batteries. One EV owner did the math after two months of EV ownership and came up with a surprising number: $7 a month.

According to recent reports, whether we’re talking gasoline, diesel, or electricity, one driver’s fuel costs can look dramatically different from another’s. How far they drive, how often, and under what conditions can matter just as much as what they drive. And while EVs may offer the greatest benefits to rural drivers covering long distances, a Redditor going by Suitable-Truth-350 took a different approach, moving into a highly walkable city for the express purpose of driving as little as possible.

“My wife and I recently retired and moved from a car dependent, rural/suburban area to a large, walkable city with good light rail. Our goal was to drive as little as possible,” write Suitable-Truth-350. “We took delivery of an Ioniq5 in August. We still have a daily walking life, but we use the car to see friends in the country, shop or travel around the greater Chicagoland area. After 2 months, we finally charged it.”.

It has been revealed that the result? Suitable says it took less than 30 minutes to juice their Ioniq 5 back up to an 80% SOC, at a total cost of $13.

“Driving the car is a pleasure,” they continue. “The pickup and smooth operation so different from our last ICE vehicle. First impression, we love the car and could never imagine going back to (a gasoline-powered car).”.

I’ve been saying it for years: drive an EV for a week and whatever range anxiety you might experience will disappear. And, while it seems like Suitable-Truth-350 didn’t have much range anxiety to begin with, it’s worth noting here that their situation isn’t that rare.

In their most recent national survey, AAA found that the average US driver covered less than 29 miles per day, with the vast majority weekly commuting totals falling well within the range of even the most affordable used EVs.

The same survey found that just 30% of Americans reported taking at least one road trip the previous summer, with an average one-way trip length of ~235 miles.

That 235 mile trip might be too much for a car like the Fiat 500e, but even that car – the new EV with the shortest EPA-estimated range you can buy in the US – can make a 235 mile trip with a single 30-minute stop to charge. And in 2026 and 2027, they’re sure to find plenty of places to charge, thanks to a public charging network that’s newer, faster, and far more built out than they probably think, with more fast-charging locations opening every week and modern charging speeds that make longer stops the exception instead of the norm.

Recent findings suggest that our two EVs raised our monthly electric bill by ~ $60/mo. and that's without solar. That wouldn't have paid for one gas fill-up for a week in our previous gas cars. I don't think this is even a question. If you can charge at home, it's cheaper. If you rely on public charging all the time then it's a mixed bag but still generally cheaper in most parts of the country. All mentioned, we have three EVs now and my monthly electric bill for our entire house with six people is less than what we paid for fuel in one gas car.

In other words: your charging costs are probably going to be higher than Suitable-Truth-350’s seven-ish dollars per month, but with $4/gallon premium and $6/gallon diesel still very much the norm in 2026, it’ll probably be less than you think, too.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Tai 9 is a six-seat, plug-in hybrid SUV about the same size as the Cadillac Escalade IQ, and it sits at the top of the Fangchengbao range.
  • Power comes from two electric motors that produce 536 horsepower at peak, while a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine is responsible for any combustion-powered driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have to admit that when I first saw the Fangchengbao Tai 9 stow its steering wheel away on social media, I assumed that it was AI. It wasn't. This BYD brand's new SUV can indeed retract its steering wheel right into the dashboard. However, it’s not quite used for the reason you’d think.

Sources indicate that the Tai 9 is a six-seat, plug-in hybrid SUV about the same size as the Cadillac Escalade IQ, and it sits at the top of the Fangchengbao range. BYD’s Chinese-market brand and naming structure can be confusing, but in essence, Fangchengbao is one of BYD's premium brands.

Power comes from two electric motors that produce 536 horsepower at peak, while a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine is responsible for any combustion-powered driving. The Tai 9 has a 66.5 kWh battery that is capable of BYD’s flash charging technology. The brand claims it can sprint from 10% to 97% in nine minutes.

It has been revealed that those are all very compelling specs, but the most interesting part of the Tai 9 is the top-of-the-line Foldable Smart Cabin trim. Since the Tai 9 uses a steer-by-wire system, the steering wheel can fold up and stow itself in the dashboard. BYD notes that takes about 10 seconds.

Sources indicate that however, this isn’t for any sort of autonomous driving. China’s autonomous driving rules are strict, and no automaker in the country has approval for commercially sold eyes-off, hands-off driver assist features. Instead, the folding steering wheel is primarily for comfort and space, specifically when the car is stationary. Photos of the feature in action show that stowing away the steering wheel makes extra room for a little table setup.

In a recent development, this isn’t entirely unprecedented. The new trend in China is for large SUVs to be third spaces where buyers can comfortably hang out, even when they aren't driving. The Tai 9’s Nappa leather, comfy seats, and second-row folding screen are meant to make it a calming, relaxing space to spend time. It's similar in concept to what we’ve seen on the Zeekr Mix and SkyNomad N90 Studio.

Still, despite the Tai 9’s folding steering wheel not being for self-driving, I wouldn’t be surprised if it does show up in cars for that reason someday, as manufacturers strive to make cars that can truly drive themselves.

A car with no steering wheel at all might feel risky and uncomfortable to some car buyers, especially if it's like Tesla’s Cybercab, which can’t be driven manually at all above low speeds. Yet, if there were a backup to take control, I could see that putting some minds at ease.

The Fangchengbao Tai 9 is on sale in China for about $42,000. The top-of-the-line model with the foldable steering wheel is about $49,500.

Whether her in-game body type will actually let her put that strength out on the pitch (she will surely also have Bruiser) remains to be seen, but she could easily have the gangly aura of Patrick Vieira if the rest of her PlayStyles are right.

New Ultimate Team Heroes have been added mid-season before, including the likes of Enzo Francescoli in FC 24, but 3 at once looks to indicate that EA is leaning on Heroes to add fan-favourite players to the game with a lower threshold than Icons.

Plus they can be given away for free without upsetting the power curve as much as Icons, as shown by the free Classic XI Heroes handed out recently (I got Mario Gomez, F).

The rest of the Winter Wildcards team features a host of equally famous, and now infamous, players with some featuring 99 stats and alternative positions.

#120904. Tesla releases FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1300 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla releases FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.
  • Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a upcoming live visualization that looks seriously impressive.
  • Tesla unveiled the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.

Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a upcoming live visualization that looks seriously impressive. If the driving improvements are as real as the visuals, this is a substantial update.

Tesla unveiled the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes. The organization didn’t say which vehicles get it first, but it has previously told investors that its AI4 (HW4) computer is enough to run v15.

Here are Tesla’s release notes for FSD v15:.

It has been revealed that v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:.

Tesla’s main announcement also says FSD can now slow down for speed cameras, and it adds Bike Rack Mode, which allows FSD with a bike rack or a similar hitch accessory. Navigation learning only covers the start and end of trips for now; Tesla says later v15 releases will expand it to the entire route.

According to recent reports, the new visualization is the flashiest part, and based on the video Tesla shared, it’s super impressive. The center screen indicates a detailed, rendered version of the street around the car, far beyond the current FSD visualization.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW.

Tesla calls it “Reality View” in its announcement and “Tesla Augmented Reality” in the release notes. The notes say it replaces all the separate model signals with a single end-to-end visualization that uses less compute, and Tesla says it lets the driver “see & control what FSD is planning to do.” If that works as advertised, it could make supervising the system a lot easier.

According to recent reports, what stands out more is where Tesla is focusing. Almost every driving improvement in the release notes targets an area where FSD struggles today.

Signs are a significant one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen demonstrated a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

It has been revealed that potholes are another. In August, Musk noted pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them.

School zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

So if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

According to recent reports, one change goes the other way. Tesla notes it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

Industry observers note that the release notes clear up what the “25x” refers to: Tesla claims the upcoming vision encoder improves the critical intervention rate by 25x. That’s the right metric to measure progress toward unsupervised driving. But Tesla still doesn’t share the actual number, only the multiplier.

Industry observers note that the math gets interesting fast. Our data from earlier this year suggested FSD v14 could go a couple thousand miles between critical interventions. A 25x improvement on that would put v15 around 50,000 miles between critical interventions, well beyond the roughly 10,000 miles we’ve mentioned Tesla needs for a limited unsupervised service. If that were true across the fleet, we could see Tesla having its most meaningful push toward autonomy in a long time.

And v15 already carries plenty of hype. In April, Elon Musk wrote that v15 “will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.” We pointed out at the time that he had said similar things about v12 and v14. In August, Tesla told JPMorgan that v15 is a “step-change” built on seven “core technologies,” with about 40% of them already running in its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

Industry observers note that FSD has never improved in a straight line. Every major version has brought real gains along with fresh problems, and point releases regularly go backward.

Recent findings suggest that when v14 arrived in October 2025, it came with hallucinations, brake stabbing, and excessive speeding, and early crowdsourced data revealed about 732 miles between critical disengagements, below what we expected. It then improved a lot. Then the v14.2 updates went backward before Musk sold v14.3 as the version where “the last significant piece of the puzzle finally lands.”.

Seven months and a long string of point releases later, owners are still supervising, and Tesla now needs v15 to deliver what v14.3 was supposed to.

I remain skeptic of Tesla's autonomous driving until they apply for the California DMV permit to begin testing autonomous driving without a driver. California is a significant enough of a potential market for robotaxi that Tesla is operating a human driver taxi service. The common presumption is that Tesla is avoiding California autonomous testing because it requires disclosing critical interventions and other data which wouldn't be favorable to Tesla's claims.

The visuals are super impressive. That much we can already judge from the video, and Reality View could make FSD easier to understand and supervise.

The driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good update.

According to recent reports, but “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1702 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification.
  • ENHANCEMENT 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.
  • According to recent reports, “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that america’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

ENHANCEMENT 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

According to recent reports, “An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”.

Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any newly introduced ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

When you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

Industry observers note that country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

What’s more, a newly introduced wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

It has been revealed that with only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

Recent findings suggest that unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

Sources indicate that if disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

If you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

In a recent development, it’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

According to recent reports, at the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

And while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some new, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility manufacturer to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

In a recent development, that mentioned, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

Las Vegas Grand Prix Delivers 50 Laps of Close Battles While Verstappen Holds On to Win

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Max Verstappen started on pole for the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday evening and held the lead at one point on every lap, but the race was far more thrilling than that would let on.
  • Verstappen qualified second and inherited pole after pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli received a five-place grid penalty.
  • At the start, Max Verstappen took the lead from George Russell and kept his elbows out as he had the hardest spot on the track, punching through the crisp air with no help from a slipstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Max Verstappen started on pole for the Las Vegas Grand Prix on Saturday evening and held the lead at one point on every lap, but the race was far more thrilling than that would let on.

Verstappen qualified second and inherited pole after pole-sitter Kimi Antonelli received a five-place grid penalty.

At the start, Max Verstappen took the lead from George Russell and kept his elbows out as he had the hardest spot on the track, punching through the crisp air with no help from a slipstream.

On the second lap of the race, Russell, in a much faster Mercedes, passed Verstappen in the final corners coming off the Las Vegas Strip straight, then lost the lead before the first corner of the next lap. He would repeat this multiple times throughout the first half of the Grand Prix.

The race recorded a record 35 lead changes, but no one could cement a run past Verstappen.

With Verstappen slowing the field behind him, the first 10 laps of the race found the top three within one second and the top ten within less than 4.5 seconds.

On lap 20, Sergio Perez tried to make a pick on Rafeal Camera and the Haas, and Cadillac ended up tangled in the barrier, bringing out a full safety car. In a normal race, this would’ve neutralized the race, but with everyone still running bunched up, it just sent the field all together to the pits, leading to teams double-stacking against each other.

Hamilton was the biggest loser at the pit stop, having to serve a 10-second penalty that was not yet shared with him for a battle with Norris that he thought was just.

Hamilton was kept out while everyone else pitted to clear space for Charles Leclerc and was told about his penalty.

It has been revealed that “Ah, that’s shit. If I turned in, we would’ve crashed.”.

Under the safety car, Arvid Lindblad spun on cold tires to end his campaign for his first-ever podium. Arvid had his best starting spot of fifth for the Grand Prix and ran as high as third, while the Red Bulls on his sister team ran 1-2; he fell out of the points with the mistake.

In a recent development, shortly after racing resumed, Isack Hadjar, who challenged his teammate Verstappen for the lead in the first half of the race and often put in the hardest position between the leader and the charging field, hit debris on the track and damaged his front wing. Hadjar pitted and finished outside the points as well.

With Red Bull and VCARB drivers out of contention, the door reopened for the Mercedes as Kimi Antonelli made his way into the picture following his grid drop, and Russell never left.

With two laps to go, Antonelli led Russell as the teammate fought for second; in turn 5, Russell went for the pass, overcommitted, and slid into the barrier.

Verstappen laughed on from ahead following a weekend of tension between the front-row starters.

Antonelli fell away from the lead battle on the penultimate lap with an internal matter and would come home fourth.

Recent findings suggest that in the mayhem, the McLarens saw their luck change at Las Vegas. Following this double disqualification while battling for the championship last year, Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri walked away with a shocking first double podium of the season.

“I led for about 15 seconds, so I’m very proud,” Norris joked.

Antonelli was followed by Pierre Gasly, Franco Colapinto, Lewis Hamilton, Carlos Sainz, George Russell and Charles Leclerc in the points-paying positions.

This Plug-In Hybrid SUV Towed A Boeing 747 On Only 2 Wheels. Yes, Really.
