#120874. Tech Report: Zelda Ocarina Remake Producers Talk Changing And Maintaining The Game, Easter Eggs, The Bombchu Bowling Alley Operator, And More

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Zelda Ocarina Remake Producers Talk Changing And Maintaining The Game, Easter Eggs, The Bombchu Bowling Alley Operator, And More

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today marks the release of the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2.
  • Topics include how the team approached remaking Ocarina of Time, what needed changing and what needed to stay the same, their thoughts on the Easter Eggs from the original game, the fate and marital status of the Bombchu Bowling girl, and more.
  • The discussion covers a fairly faithful remake of Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, which debuted nearly 30 years ago, but I have spoiler-marked certain questions and answers that might be considered sensitive if you want to maintain surprise when playing the remake yourself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today marks the release of the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. You can read my full, positive review here. Ahead of the game’s release, but after having played the game to completion (well… 99% as you will learn below), I traveled to New York to speak with Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma (whose work on the original Ocarina of Time marked his first involvement with the series) and Ocarina of Time remake producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi (director of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom among other Zelda titles).

Topics include how the team approached remaking Ocarina of Time, what needed changing and what needed to stay the same, their thoughts on the Easter Eggs from the original game, the fate and marital status of the Bombchu Bowling girl, and more.

The discussion covers a fairly faithful remake of Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, which debuted nearly 30 years ago, but I have spoiler-marked certain questions and answers that might be considered sensitive if you want to maintain surprise when playing the remake yourself.

Mr. Fujibayashi, what is your relationship to Ocarina of Time?

Fujibayashi: Regarding the original Ocarina of Time, at the time I was working for a different tech giant, so it was mainly me as an end user trying to looking forward to the experience of what a 3D Zelda is going to look like. So, really, I was just waiting in anticipation for that.

How long has the remake been in development?

Sources indicate that aonuma: It's actually kind of hard to say exactly when development began because the earliest thought process was us thinking about the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda approaching, and so we started to have this conversation, “Oh, what should we make to mark this occasion?” And then at that point, we decided on Ocarina of Time, and so a lot of time elapsed from the beginning of that conversation about the anniversary until we got to Ocarina. So it's hard to pinpoint exactly when the development itself began.

Was this a more relaxing game to develop after making Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom back-to-back?

Aonuma: Was it relaxing? That's kind of a hard question to ask. I would say it's more a different style of development. So, if we looked at Tears of the Kingdom, Breath of the Wild, these were created as new games with a very different kind of development cycle. Whereas for a remake like this one, we decided to take an interesting approach, which is to bring in this new younger staff and find out what they would bring to this project in terms of their own experience, their own interpretation as newer staff.

And so my role here was really advising them on this, and it's not always like the development cycle of a latest game. But in one sense, the producer has to be careful not to advise too much, to say that you must do it like this. You don't want to prescribe the approach that anyone is going to take. You want to make sure that there's enough space for these younger staff members to have their own interpretation, their own approach to it.

Do you have remake philosophies or rules, like what needs to stay the same and what should change?

Sources indicate that fujibayashi: So, in fact, there were pretty clear kind of rules or guidelines, as you noted. First, is because you know, as Mr. Aonuma had mentioned, where he wanted to, the development team was centered around the young directors that took part in this development. And when we first started discussing what kind of game and what kind of approach you wanted to take. One thing that really came through and we clarified was, as you mentioned, what are we going to change and what are we going to keep the same.

It has been revealed that and I'll start with what we wanted to change, and that was really to make sure that – because we have the ability to use the latest technology through the Nintendo Switch 2 – there's a lot we can change and improve upon, such as you know obviously things like controls, graphics. We also have a latest controller, so that allows for the new camera controls. And we’re really able to fine tune and polish the feel of the game and there was excitement for all the ways of expression we can provide the player.

Industry observers note that but on the other hand, thinking about what we didn't want to change, we were thinking about the creators of the original Ocarina of Time, and what they wanted to convey, the experience that they wanted to provide for users and players through this title. That's something that we wanted to keep intact and that spirit to carry across. And we wanted to make sure that this fresh game is able to deliver that in the way that we wanted them to.

According to recent reports, aonuma: So speaking as someone who worked on the original Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, you always have those moments looking back of, “Oh, you know, I really wanted to do more of this,” or, “I wanted to be able to express this in a different way,” but you're faced with certainly the tech limitations of the time. And I went on from Ocarina of Time to work on other Zelda franchise titles, as well. And with each new title, you're always looking for a new way to express something that may not have been available to you previously. But you always have to keep in mind is what makes a Zelda game special, and how do we protect that? How do we keep that in store for the players, as well. So, on this project in particular, I had to think of that through the lens of how do we protect the things that make it the Zelda Ocarina experience, but also how do I give the freedom to the staff to find their own expression of these ideas? And I think between those two things, we found a really good balance. So I'm very happy about that.

When we interviewed you, Mr. Aonuma, for Game Informer’s Breath of the Wild cover story, Shigeru Miyamoto was present, and he made a joke about the challenge of the water temple. Are you happy with where the Water Temple is now in the remake?

Industry observers note that aonuma: Certainly, looking back on the challenge level of the Water Temple, I think it was hard, but some of that came from the system that we were presenting to players. So, for example, if you look at the way that players used to have to switch to the heavy iron boots so that they could sink in the water, you had to go to a different screen and press the button. But now that we're able to give players a shortcut, single button on the gameplay screen, I think they can get to that more rapidly. It's a better experience because they can focus on solving the puzzle rather than having to navigate menus and thinking about that and interrupting the flow of their thought each time.

Another consideration compared to the original is that you couldn't move the camera angle in the original game, and so if you were looking for a certain room in this 3D space relative to where you are now, it was much more difficult to orient yourself and think about the space where that room might exist. So I think those two together, you know, also with the heavy boots being one button press, I think this, for me, is the best version of the Water Temple.

It has been revealed that is the canon of the Zelda timeline considered at all during development? Did you think about adding in Easter eggs that made references to things that would have happened later in the Zelda story? Like Wind Waker taking place after Ocarina of Time, for example.

Industry observers note that aonuma: It's funny because the staff would sometimes ask me about the possibility of including nods to the timeline or references to the other game, and I actually, at the time, would say, "No, let's focus on this game. Let's make this the best version of Ocarina of Time that we can." So, the timeline was in the back of our mind, but we didn't consider taking an approach to this game where we actually, explicitly included references like that.

When testing the game, was it challenging to find people who had never played Ocarina of Time?

It has been revealed that aonuma: As it turns out, both on our staff and in the testing teams, there's a lot of young people, and many of them had never played the original. So it wasn't a challenge to find them.

In a recent development, who do you primarily consider this remake to be for? New people who have never played Ocarina? Or fans like myself who consider it to be, frankly, their favorite game. Who is the key audience?

Fujibayashi: The answer is both. Our response to those fans who have fond memories of this title is really what I mentioned earlier: being able to provide the experience of what it was like to play Ocarina of Time back to them, and that was our response to them. And when it comes to the players that are experiencing this for the first time, whether it's the graphics, or the controls, or the ability to shift and move the camera; those are all changes and fine-tuning that we've made to make sure that people who are used to modern gaming are able to enter this experience with as little friction as possible. So again, to answer your question? It's really both.

It has been revealed that aonuma: Certainly, when you look at the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, there is so much hidden in the world that people spend a lot of time looking for things. And your first time playing through, you may not find all of it in one go. People in that kind of situation would refer to strategy books and information that they can find.

For example, when you're looking for the like last Skulltala and you already have 99, our job is to think about how to give the player an approach to that sort of a problem. What kind of information can we give them to help out. To make it a fun, but still challenging experience, because we want even new players to come in and to be able to fully experience this world that we've created for them, even though old fans are going to come in with a little bit of an advantage in the form of a lot of prior game knowledge.

Sources indicate that I'm not kidding about needing some help with that final Skulltala. I'm going to hand you my Switch 2 after this so you can show me where it is because it's been driving me crazy. I've been having dreams about where the final Skulltala might be.

The end of the game in the remake made me emotional in a way I wasn't expecting. It made me cry, just the whole ending of the experience overall. Were you expecting that kind of reaction from players?

Recent findings suggest that fujibayashi: So first, I want to say I'm very, very happy and excited to hear you say that because, as you mentioned, that cutscene – cutscenes in general – but that cutscene specifically is something that we, as a dev team, heavily discussed. Because of the limitations of the technology back in the day, there might have been things that we weren't able to convey fully, whether it's because of the tempo of the game… whatever it is. And so, when we approached this remake, we wanted to make sure that we captured that moment in the way that we wanted to express it. So that the right kinds of emotions are evoked, and that we can convey the emotion and the story that we wanted to at that moment. And now that hearing you say that and kind of having that reaction really struck a chord? I'm really relieved to hear that because that's exactly what we wanted to do.

You’re relieved that you made me cry?

Sources indicate that the ReDeads, the Shadow Temple, the Dead Hand miniboss, Wall Masters – these enemies traumatized a whole generation of kids. I'm curious if that was always the intention and how did you approach making sure that those elements still remained scary? Was there a line that was too scary?

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, we had this intent to make sure that we allow the players to find the enemies a little bit scary. They have to be, right? We want to express that sort of thing. But more than anything, they are part of this Fantasy world, which has both light and dark portions, and so we're trying to bring that feeling across. It’s not that we're trying to scare people outright as the entire intent, but rather show that you know Link is part of a brighter part of the world where people are friendly, and Ganon is a part of the darker part of the world where there's a lot of scary things. And we kept that in mind in the remake as well.

We wanted to make sure we were bringing that out, but the tools that we have available to us now for expression are so capable that if we really tried, of course, we could make something that was very, very scary. But this is supposed to be for all kinds of players. We didn't want to hit the scary notes so strongly that we were putting off new players or younger players, and so we want to have that tuning very carefully in mind as we're making those adjustments in terms of presenting that final expression in the game.

I shudder to visualize what the scarier versions of the ReDeads might look like.

Aonuma: What was your experience of them this time?

Oh, terrifying! That noise. The noise they make. That scream. I feel it in my chest. It just recalls that scariness of my childhood in a way that I admit is very entertaining, and I like. Do you remember recording that sound effect? How did you do that? Did you have someone scream?

Aonuma: Sorry, I don't recall [laughs].

Recent findings suggest that for the remake, a lot has been rewritten. The meaning hasn't been changed dramatically, but pretty much everything has been rewritten. What was the goal with the rewriting overall?

Sources indicate that fujibayashi: Yes, it's as you stated. We did a lot of rewriting of the text. When it comes to the original Ocarina of Time, there's the idea that because it was 28 years ago – it's a long time ago – there's the turn of phrase, or the way it's been written, is sometimes not clear or doesn't work in the modern day, given the context of the modern day. And so that's why we wanted to make sure that it makes sense and it's easier to understand for people who are familiar with playing modern games, and also that it works better here.

And when you think about… obviously the graphics have been improved significantly. Before we had to do things like… “That blue ocarina that is the size that you could fit on a hand,” something like that, to make sure that the idea gets across to the player. But now, because the graphics are improved, it's very clear what the size it is. It's very clear that it's a blue ocarina. So with the latest graphics, if you go through the wordy explanation of what it is, the player is going to be like, "Yeah, I can see it." So in order to make sure that we remove those kind of slight hurdles and really make sure that we can present the game and improve not only the expression but also the pacing of the game? That's something that we really took into consideration as we were rewriting the game.

According to recent reports, I wanted to ask about some specific changes for the remake. You get five bottles now. Why?

Aonuma: Because bottles are so important to the way the player plays the game, like looking for strategies to deal with different kinds of situations, even at the time of development of the original title, I thought, “Oh, you know, I could do with even just one more bottle.” I think certainly when you collect all four in the original, you feel great about that at time. But I was still thinking like one more would be okay, right?

It has been revealed that so, all this time that was in the back of my mind. But when the latest younger staff were familiarizing themselves with the old game and thinking about what they might want to change in this version, one thing that I suggested was that the player could get their first bottle earlier, and this would actually be really useful in terms of reinforcing for the player how helpful bottles were and motivating them on their quest to find the next bottle. It strengthens that whole sequence through the game by changing the order just a little bit there. But yeah, certainly, once you have a certain number of bottles, you're going to feel a little bit more confident and more comfortable. But reinforcing that feeling early on, I think, was important for us in the development of this one.

In the original, there were Nintendo character portraits in Zelda's courtyard of Mario, Yoshi, and more, but those have been removed. I was curious as to why.

Industry observers note that aonuma: Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing. But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, "Why is Yoshi there?” We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time.

However, you will remember that there is one design element on Talon with Bowser on it, and that's part of the original design of the character. So we didn't change that. That stays as is.

I have some short-answer questions. The woman who runs the Bombchu Bowling game. What happened to her after seven years. And is she single?

Aonuma: That's something we're not going to touch, and I'll leave it to your imagination.

One of the Skulltala rewards is Bombchus, which I found disappointing when I was young, and I found disappointing as an adult. Why does he give you Bombchus?

Industry observers note that aonuma: So that feeling you had when you got, as a reward for a certain number of Skulltalas, the Bombchus, and you thought, “Wait, that's it?” That's also part of the original experience of the 64 version. So there, there's an approach that we take where we try to keep all of the different notes that people felt in the original game in place. You know, sometimes it's really remarkable, fun things, and other times it's slight moments of disappointment. Even that could be memorable in that way. It's vital to maintain that.

In a recent development, the Great Fairies. What do they need rupees for?

Fujibayashi: You know, it's really about a feeling. It's like in Japan sometimes, like donations to a temple or something similar like that. It's to express your reverence for the great fairies.

In a recent development, the 3DS remake had Skyward Sword art hidden in a couple of places, but you removed it for this remake. You didn't want to keep the Skyward Sword art?

In a recent development, aonuma: [Laughs] I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I noted, “Okay, sure.” But like earlier when we were talking about in the courtyard sequence with the Yoshi portrait. You know, you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Fujibayashi, you directed Skyward Sword. Were you sad to see that reference removed?

Industry observers note that fujibayashi: [Laughs] No, it’s really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there.

I think the biggest cutscene change in the game is when Link transitions from child to adult. It is now a much more involved sequence. Why did that scene need such a drastic change?

Aonuma: So I think that's really connected to the way we were thinking about expressing things in the original. We couldn't do everything. We couldn't express everything that we'd like to, and I think in that moment where you have Ganondorf having this reaction to Link becoming older, that cutscene in the original, it was very low on explanation.

Sources indicate that so, you have these thoughts in the player's mind like, “Oh wait, why is he there? What's the relation to this process?” So, you want something that explains his presence, that explains his reaction to make a bigger impression on the player overall, and that's something that you can use to connect the motivation to want to face Ganondorf in the final fight. Something that I think comes across better now.

[I pulled out my Switch 2 and indicated them how I was missing one Skulltala in Hyrule Field].

You can see here I have 99 out of 100 and am have two out of three in Hyrule Field. Can you point to a general location to give me an idea of where to look?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is chock full of side quests that point you towards bonus hits or gang hideouts.
  • While picking up Jason’s neighbor Shirley’s rum order from a nearby liquor store, you just might hear some squawking the attendant writes off as a loud TV.
  • Sources indicate that to start, you’ll want to head to the Three Sheers Liquor store, marked on your map by Shirley when you accept her request to snag her rum order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 is chock full of side quests that point you towards bonus hits or gang hideouts. All over Leonida, groups of ner’do wells are making cash and leaving it lying around, all yours for the taking if you’re quick enough on the draw and know where to look.

While picking up Jason’s neighbor Shirley’s rum order from a nearby liquor store, you just might hear some squawking the attendant writes off as a loud TV. In reality, he’s hiding a pretty penny within an exotic animal ring run out the back, and a spiteful parrot is stuck back there ready to spill the beans. Let’s go over the quickest way to find it and run it for all its worth.

Sources indicate that to start, you’ll want to head to the Three Sheers Liquor store, marked on your map by Shirley when you accept her request to snag her rum order. Located just down the road from Jason’s place, enter for a small cutscene hinting there's more going on behind closed doors.

Once you secure Shirley’s rum in your trunk, head down the alley to the right of the store. You’ll hear a bunch of people arguing with what sounds like a parrot, insulting the crew and blabbing about hiding cash. Continue down the alley until you spot an opening in the barbed wire cover on the wall.

In a recent development, hop over, and the gang will start a brawl. Be careful, as stepping too far away will prompt multiple members to draw their guns. If you want to get out of this quietly and professionally, make sure you handle the group hand-to-hand; that way, no one calls the cops.

Once you handle all the goons, the parrot will start praising you. By interacting with it, Jason will ask about the money it mentioned, and it will start dropping hints. The important one is the generator, alluding to the small box generator in the upper left corner of the yard, behind the liquor store.

Go into focus mode, and you’ll notice a small marked crevice in the side of the store, right beside the generator. Interact with it to pocket a cool $1,382, a solid early-game sum that will more than pay for running Shirley’s errands. You can also pocket a number of melee weapons from the goons, including machetes and shovels if you’re looking for a hand-to-hand option.

The liquor store gang is one of many small, unaffiliated criminal groups that you can find throughout Leonida, acting as a great first taste of the kind of rewards that can be hiding right out of plain sight. Return Shirley’s rum, and you’ve had a very successful errand.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, has lost her seat.
  • In a recent development, upgrade: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result.
  • It has been revealed that christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, has lost her seat.

In a recent development, upgrade: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. After a recount, Chuck Hubbard has defeated Virginia Foxx by 330 votes, and will go on to represent NC-5 in Congress.

It has been revealed that christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

According to recent reports, for the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

It has been revealed that christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who said “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”.

But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily said Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”.

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

Foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In a recent development, in the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”.

According to recent reports, foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘fresh’ electric cars.”.

Recent findings suggest that but she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just new ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

Sources indicate that those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

It has been revealed that but I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

It has been revealed that he will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess reveals where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and at the moment sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article in May, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

Sources indicate that after a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district, after winning by 330 votes in a recount.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

In a recent development, generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

So they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

Foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.

But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems).

After a nail-bitingly close election, Foxx requested a recount. The margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, but today Foxx called to concede, making it the last decided House race of the election, giving Democrats a 258-seat majority.

Recent findings suggest that foxx previously vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.

#120871. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Easter Eggs That Did And Did Not Make It Into The 2026 Remake

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?).
  • Sources indicate that in the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game.
  • Industry observers note that for the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is a game full of Easter Eggs, secrets, and hidden mechanics (did you know if a butterfly lands on your Deku Stick, it summons a fairy?). Now in its second remake, not every secret has made its way forward through the previous iterations, but many have. Below you will learn about a few of the secrets that made the cut, and others that didn’t.

Sources indicate that in the courtyard where Link first meets Zelda, there is arguably the most fourth-wall-breaking Easter Egg in the whole game. If you don’t rush to Zelda and instead pause and enter first-person to look around, you will see portraits of other Nintendo characters through the windows, like Mario and Yoshi. In the 3DS remake, the portraits are replaced by an image of a Mario stage.

Industry observers note that for the 2026 remake, there are no references to other Nintendo characters. Instead, the tapestry you build over the course of the game is on display. Removing the reference to Nintendo characters outside of the Zelda universe is understandable, but it is a little odd that art representing the full adventure of the game – an adventure that has not yet concluded – is on the wall.

According to recent reports, as stated above, the Nintendo character portraits are gone, but there is still a guard you can annoy. If you fire a Deku Seed into the left window, a guard will pop out, yell at you, and then throw a bomb at you. You can’t pick up the bomb. In fact, at this point in the game, you haven’t even seen a bomb.

The Hyrule Castle portrait references to Yoshi and Mario are gone (though Mario and Luigi are still kind of in the game in a way), but Bowser gets a pass for some reason. Both Malon and her dad, Talon, are still wearing Bowser pins on their clothes. And unlike the N64 game where the detail was a little vague, there is no mistaking it here.

Gossip Stones are all over Ocarina of Time and it takes a while to understand what they do. If you hit them with a sword, they tell you the time, and if you play Zelda’s Lullaby near them, they refill your magic. If you do the Happy Mask Salesman’s side quest, interacting with them while wearing the Mask of Truth offers little hints and details about the world. But then there are interactions that are just odd for no reason. Blowing up a bomb near a Gossip Stone still makes it take off like a rocket ship, and using the Megaton Hammer still flattens them for a moment like a Looney Tunes.

And speaking of playing Zelda’s Lullaby for inanimate objects, if you slash a sign to pieces with your sword and regret your words and deeds, you can play the iconic tune to make the signs reform and become readable again.

This detail was exclusive to the 3DS remake of Ocarina of Time, and surprising no one, it has been removed. Ocarina of Time released in June 2011 and Nintendo released Skyward Sword about five months later in November. For… marketing purposes, I guess, Skyward Sword art could be found in Lonlon Ranch, the Bombchu Shop in Hyrule Castle Town, and the Gerudo Fortress. It was a fun Easter Egg to discover back in 2011, especially since Skyward Sword was still months away, but these days it’s a bit of an odd inclusion.

Though never explicit, the composer ghosts guarding the Sun’s Song (and Link’s first ReDead encounter) have always been assumed to be inspired by Mario and Luigi. They are brothers; Flat is short, squat, and red; Sharp is lanky and green. They still appear in Ocarina of Time this way, which isn't surprising, since they are notable characters you must meet to get a very useful song. Fans have also speculated that Talon and Ingo are Mario and Luigi-inspired for similar reasons, but it’s worth noting that they are not brothers.

In the Spirit Temple there is a large statue of a woman and for reasons that have never been explained, Link could attach his hookshot to her breasts. It served no purpose. It didn’t help solve a puzzle. If anything, it was confusing. But we all tried it and there is no shame in admitting it! That was removed for the 3DS remake, and it remains removed in 2026.

Industry observers note that this is a very subtle reference to Wind Waker/Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom and is potentially the only addition to the remake that looks toward the future of the Zelda franchise. Obviously, plenty of characters in Ocarina later appear in Majora’s Mask (another remake of that is hopefully being considered), but it would be inaccurate to call those intentional Easter Eggs.

However, in Kokiri Forest and in the neighboring Lost Woods, the magical debris floating in the air often resembles a Korok as it would later appear in the series. It makes sense, too, because the Koroks are meant to be what the Kokiri transformed into following The Great Flood.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience introduces today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside upgrade 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

It has been revealed that the beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

It has been revealed that the Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

According to recent reports, the Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

It has been revealed that the Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that riot will take the Mid-Season Invitational to Spain in 2027, bringing a top-tier League of Legends event back to Europe for the first time since the Worlds 2024 final in London. Its one-off, expanded First Stand in China will also change Split 1 for the LEC, with the full details due in January.

Europe will host a top-tier League of Legends event again in 2027. Riot set out its international calendar on 13 November, the eve of the Worlds 2026 final. The Mid-Season Invitational goes to Valencia. London’s staging of the Worlds 2024 final was the last time the continent held an international League of Legends tournament.

For British fans, that puts a top-tier event within Europe next year. Riot has not yet given dates or ticket details for the Feria de Valencia event.

It has been revealed that spain’s last international League of Legends event came in 2019. That year, Madrid’s Palacio Vistalegre staged the Worlds quarter-finals and semi-finals. Valencia has never hosted one before.

Recent findings suggest that china will stage First Stand: All In at the start of the 2027 season. Riot calls this single edition its largest tournament ever.

First Stand 2027 had originally been given to Southeast Asia. The bigger format took it to China instead. Southeast Asia will now host the event in 2028.

The change reaches every regional league, including the LEC. The larger event will change Split 1, just as Fnatic, G2 and the other LEC teams rebuild their rosters. In 2026, First Stand ran from 16 to 22 March, between the two regional splits. A bigger event at the start of the year leaves less certainty about how that window will look in 2027.

Industry observers note that riot has not yet said how many teams will take part or how they will qualify. Until then, LEC teams are building squads without knowing how many European places are on offer.

Worlds 2027 will be shared between two countries. The Swiss Stage goes to Nagoya, Japan. The quarter-finals and semi-finals move to the Suwon Convention Center in South Korea. The title decider goes to Seoul Arena, which is still under construction.

The arena was 81% built on 23 October. Work is due to finish in May 2027, with the venue opening in June 2027.

Sources indicate that the city is backing the event with public money. Seoul has set aside 1.369 billion won (about US$1.02 million) in its proposed 2027 budget to host the Worlds final and Fan Fest, Sheep Esports reported.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that peel the name tags off the Mazda Cosmo, and it could easily pass for an American car.
  • The Cosmo is something of a mystery car.
  • Industry observers note that that’s the situation in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the April 1977 problem of Car and Driver.

Sources indicate that peel the name tags off the Mazda Cosmo, and it could easily pass for an American car. The two-rotor Wankel is as smooth and vibra­tionless as any V-8, the car is easily as quiet inside as a typical intermediate sedan, and the Cosmo’s body even has the same sort of creaky flexibility that we’ve come to expect of Detroit cars. If we didn’t know better, we might think this was a upcoming subcompact Buick or perhaps a miniature Camaro. Never would we confuse it with a Toyota or Datsun.

The Cosmo is something of a mystery car. It was designed with the United States in mind—a fast, smooth sports coupe for a country that swallowed Datsun Z-cars as fast as the ships could unload them at the ports. But for some reason, the Cosmo never struck the American fancy. Maybe it was the bad publicity heaped on the rotary engine; per­haps the dull colors and unfortunate combi­nation of mag wheels and white-wall tires turned off the sporty-car buyer. And we can’t entirely disregard the thought that a coupe with a Vega silhouette, Oldsmobile waterfall grille, and Plymouth Cricket taillights may sim­ply be the wrong thing to wave in American faces. But whatever the reason, Cosmos tend to languish in the showrooms.

See all results for used cars for sale near 55952.

Industry observers note that that’s the situation in the U.S. In Japan, the Cosmo is last season’s smash hit, named Car of the Year by one of the country’s auto mag­azines and the next best thing in Tokyo to driving a foreign car. (The Japanese, like many Americans, tend to think that anything imported is probably better and certainly more fun than the made-at-home equivalent). The car looks great in its own neighborhood. It has slightly different—but not much small­er—bumpers and the mandatory mirrors perched out on the front fenders halfway to the headlights. But apart from those two de­tails, the Japanese-market Cosmo looks the same as the one we tend to ignore here.

We humbly submit, at this point, that the Cosmo deserves another look, if for no other reason than it features one commodity in de­cidedly short supply elsewhere—horsepower. This car is quick. The engine is wide awake above 2000 rpm, and it climbs to 7000 with­out a backward glance. Freeways abound with legions of 350 four-barrels that won’t match the Cosmo’s pace. And as amazing as it may seem, none of them can come close to the Mazda’s gas mileage. The 1977 model with the standard five-speed trans­mission has been weaned down to 32 mpg highway and 20 mpg city for a combined rating of 25 mpg in the EPA mileage sweep­stakes. That is excellent economy for a car of this performance level.

While the Cosmo is surprisingly economical, it is by no means austere. The interior offers about the same amount of useful space for four occupants as a Camaro, and the trunk, because it stows its spare more ef­ficiently than the Chevrolet, is at least as good. Yet overall, the Mazda Cosmo is about the same size as a Corvette, actually slightly smaller.

See all results for used cars for sale near 55952.

According to recent reports, the quality of the interior is also on par with that of Detroit models. The dash is molded vinyl with a minimum of seams, and shows the driver a full complement of instruments set in a field of imitation wood. Velour cloth covers the seats and door panels. There is even a trapezoid opera window to delight the double-knit crowd. And if that doesn’t knock them dead at the Donut Center, show them the wire-spoked steering wheel.

There is just one aspect of the Mazda’s er­satz Detroit personality with which we take is­sue: It’s a smooth-road car. On ribbons of un­broken concrete the Cosmo simply glides along, but when the going gets rough, so does the ride. The front wheels steer notice­ably over bumps, and the suspension travel is limited enough so that the wheels are occa­sionally jerked clear of the road on surfaces that are not really that rough. The balance of the car, particularly on smooth roads, is rea­sonable however.

According to recent reports, at least the Cosmo’s ailments are the kind that can be fixed, certainly by a second look at the factory and perhaps even with a few bolt-on aftermarket parts. We would start with the shocks and see what happens. The rotary engine, on the other hand, is just fine as it is. And Mazda provides an incredible warranty—­five years or 75,000 miles—to make sure it stays that way. Nobody can dislike a car that is guaranteed to keep running even after the loan is paid off.

Tech Report: The Switch 2 Pro Controller Can Make Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Even Better

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time hit Switch 2 today, and, as Kyle Hilliard pointed out in our review, it is pretty excellent. Along with its remarkable visual upgrade, the new Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time adds quality-of-life improvements and modernizes the control scheme. As part of that, Nintendo has added the ability to jump and sprint. While that works well to make the game feel new, I rapidly realized it sometimes clashes with another new improvement: a free camera controlled by the right stick. Holding down the sprint button to get through areas as fast as possible can make it tricky to keep the camera where you want it, but thankfully, if you have the Switch 2 Pro Controller, there's an easy fix.

After hours of running around, I was awestruck by the level of detail and updates, but I found myself constantly fighting with the camera, or at the very least, needing to take a strange claw-style grip to be able to direct the camera with the right stick, while holding down the A button to sprint. If you're a casual Switch 2 player, you might not have even noticed the back buttons on the Pro Controller, or you just have no idea what they do. Those buttons can be remapped on a per-game basis and it's a simple process. Everyone has their own preferences, but, for example, for high-mobility shooters, I like remapping one of those to reload and one to jump. I've never felt the need to remap in a Zelda game, but after feeling the need to do so with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, I might do so going forward.

If you, like me, struggle to comfortably steer the fresh free camera while running through hallways, towns, dungeons, and, yes, Hyrule Field, you might want to consider remapping your controller. As you can see in the above image, the placement of Jump and Dash on the face buttons can make it difficult to simultaneously control the camera and sprint. This isn't typically a problem in most modern games, as clicking the right stick is often a toggle to sprint, but in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, you need to hold the button.

Sources indicate that if you have the Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller, copying one button's functionality to the buttons on the back of the controller is simple. All you need to do is hold the Home button on the Switch 2 Pro Controller for a moment until the Switch 2 system menu appears on the right side. Along with Power Options and any Bluetooth audio devices you have available, there is also the option to map GL and GR, the controller's back buttons on the left and right, respectively.

Navigate down the menu to the GL and GR, then select which one you'd like to map. It will ask you which button you want to assign to the one you selected. Everyone can choose whatever makes sense in their own head, but mapping A (Roll and Dash) to GL and X (Jump) to GR made the most sense to me. Now, while I'm using the Switch 2 Pro Controller, I can use my middle finger to hold the GL button to Dash around without removing my thumb from the camera-controlling right stick.

And the best part is that, since you're not removing the functionality of the A or X buttons, you can still use them when it makes sense. For example, A also controls actions like opening up a treasure chest or door, and in my head, that feels like a face-button action, whereas rolling and dashing feel right mapped to the back buttons. The only downside is that, since this functionality is newly introduced for Switch 2 Pro Controllers, it isn't available if you're using the Joy-Cons or a Switch 1 Pro Controller. Also, it can make switching over to handheld mode challenging, as you don't have access to the back buttons in that play style.

Industry observers note that even if you don't have the ability to take advantage of this tip, either because you don't own a Switch 2 Pro Controller or because you prefer playing in handheld mode, you should still absolutely play the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. To learn more about the experience and why it's a must-play, head to our review.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering notable questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Recent findings suggest that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering notable questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Recent findings suggest that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an crucial mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

Sources indicate that the connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

Industry observers note that the consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Industry observers note that yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

Sources indicate that "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

It has been revealed that the findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," stated Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

Industry observers note that the study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Noted Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In their (slightly belated) newly introduced years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light proposal for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are presently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

According to recent reports, this, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s latest ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”.

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of fresh Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post states that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include newly introduced The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim presently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.).

According to recent reports, for a massive open-world story game like Grand Theft Auto 6, forced short playtimes can be a killer, and the constant crashes forced by error code CE-108255-1 are causing just that. Complaints across the internet say the error has no discernible cause, but it only appears on PlayStation 5 systems, leaving Xbox players in the clear.

Recent findings suggest that A recent set of firmware updates could be causing the error afflicting PS5 players, but neither Sony nor Rockstar has released any statement on it. Hopefully, as more players stumble into it, a swift hotfix patches the glitch before too many lose potentially hours of playtime to a simple bug. GTA6’s robust simulation elements would make the loss even harder, taking tons of hard work with it.

It has been revealed that no usual methods seem to help; reinstalling the game, going offline, and keeping the system cool all seem to be fruitless. Without a proper fix, players are stuck just hoping it doesn’t happen to them, a frustrating possibility that could easily tarnish their experience playing such an anticipated release.

#120857. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease.
  • Recent findings suggest that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain.
  • Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

Recent findings suggest that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the upcoming approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

Recent findings suggest that for some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

Industry observers note that "The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers.".

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells.

The upcoming technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces.".

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

In a recent development, "The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she states. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain.".

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

In a recent development, "Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an vital target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.".

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly crucial because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

It has been revealed that one possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

According to recent reports, the researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

Industry observers note that "Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately.".

Recent findings suggest that beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a latest way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward latest approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

In a recent development, with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

According to recent reports, ocarina of Time is easily one of the most notable video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power!
