💡 Key Takeaways
  • As has already been publicly revealed, DualShockers is part of The Game Awards jury, so while I have some say in which games get nominated, I am just one voice among hundreds of journalists and many, many outlets.
  • With that in mind, I put together a list of JRPGs that got snubbed at The Game Awards 2026.
  • According to recent reports, it was a massive joy to see Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter earn a nomination for Best Role Playing Game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As has already been publicly revealed, DualShockers is part of The Game Awards jury, so while I have some say in which games get nominated, I am just one voice among hundreds of journalists and many, many outlets. And just because I sit on the jury doesn't mean I agree with every outcome. Speaking from personal experience, none of the games I nominated for Game of the Year made the cut, and fair enough, my ballot was mostly JRPGs.

With that in mind, I put together a list of JRPGs that got snubbed at The Game Awards 2026. You will find titles overlooked entirely, with no nominations, alongside JRPGs that earned a spot in one category but deserved recognition in others. That isn't to say the nominees didn't earn their accolades, but as usual, JRPGs keep getting neglected at these events in favor of mainstream juggernauts that sometimes fall short of the sheer excellence found in B-side JRPGs.

According to recent reports, it was a massive joy to see Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter earn a nomination for Best Role Playing Game. I recognize that landing a Game of the Year nod would have been a tall order, and that is completely okay. However, if there is one thing the entire Trails series excels at, it is total dedication to its story, character development, and overarching narrative. With that in mind, leaving it out of Best Narrative feels borderline criminal.

Industry observers note that the entire heart of Trails beats through its storytelling. 2nd Chapter picks up right where Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter left off, expanding across Liberl and the growing threats of Ouroboros while diving intimately into each party member's backstory. It's gripping and enthralling, and even though it can occasionally be a slow burn and a bit bloated, the narrative payoff is sensational. Across all the Trails games I have played (seven so far), the series has never once missed the mark on its climaxes and final chapters, a feat worthy of serious praise.

One of the strangest choices at this year's TGAs was seeing Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave land in Best Role Playing Game, especially considering Fire Emblem Engage previously competed in Best Sim/Strategy. I heard compelling arguments from a friend suggesting that because the RPG elements in Fortune's Weave were pushed further into the spotlight, the jury may have deemed it a better fit for the RPG category. Still, I suspect it was simply an oversight.

It has been revealed that to me, it would have made far more sense for Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave to compete in Best Sim/Strategy, since being a tactical strategy RPG is the franchise's entire identity. There are two major reasons for this: first, if it hadn't taken a slot in Best RPG, another deserving JRPG could have slipped in, such as the very next entry on this list. Second, looking at the current Best Sim/Strategy lineup might leave you scratching your head, since the nominees barely seem connected to one another. What do Pokémon Pokopia, Mewgenics, and Star Wars Zero Company actually have in common? Nothing, aside from sharing a TGA category.

Following my train of thought about Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave ideally competing in Best Sim/Strategy instead of Best RPG, I could easily picture The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales sliding into that open RPG slot. I realize the title, The Adventures, might make it sound like a pure action-adventure game. Yet, Square Enix officially classifies it as an RPG, and gaming outlets generally follow suit.

Recent findings suggest that square Enix crafted an action RPG utilizing the HD-2D visual style, and the result turned out wonderfully. While its review averages hovered around 78, which explains why it missed out on nominations, I firmly believe the game deserved far more love. It is colorful and whimsical, brimming with a nostalgic sense of adventure and an intriguing narrative spanning multiple timelines (even if it completely glosses over the classic paradoxes of time travel). Then again, maybe this is just me wanting to shine a brighter spotlight on HD-2D projects so Square Enix keeps investing in smaller original IPs.

Look, I will be the first to admit that Brigandine Abyss is simply an okay game. It is solid, and I had plenty of fun clearing two campaigns, though I didn't get nearly as much mileage out of its replayability as I did with Brigandine: The Legend of Runersia. Still, since I already started ranting about the strategy genre above, I might as well throw more fuel onto a fire of my own making. Do we need a dedicated Strategy/Tactical category separated from Simulation games? Runersia. Still, since I already started ranting about the strategy genre above, I might as well add more fuel to the fire of my own making. Do we need a dedicated Strategy/Tactical category separated from Simulation games? Hard to say, though several tactical JRPGs could definitely benefit from the spotlight.

Brigandine Abyss is nothing short of a miracle, truly. The original Brigandine debuted on the PS1 and remained completely obscure, even among hardcore enthusiasts. Against all odds, Happinet revived the dormant IP with The Legend of Runersia, which apparently performed well enough to greenlight another mainline follow-up: Brigandine Abyss. If The Game Awards ever introduces a category like Second Wind or Back From the Dead, Brigandine would easily earn a spot on the ballot.

I know seeing two Trails games nominated in the same year would sound wild, especially since the franchise only recently began gaining wider global recognition thanks to its remakes, but Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter could run only because the modern mainline entries came first. Do you enjoy the seamless blend of real-time field action and command-based turn combat? That hybrid system was born in Trails through Daybreak and carried forward into every subsequent release.

Industry observers note that trails beyond the Horizon continues the overarching saga that began in Trails in the Sky, which makes it a baffling place to jump in if you haven't been following the story. That would be like starting The Lord of the Rings with The Return of the King. Nihon Falcom makes minimal effort to recap past events, yet largely assumes enthusiasts have played the earlier chapters (which is precisely why they are working so hard to remake older entries). Hopefully, in the coming years, we will see non-remake Trails entries breaking into major RPG categories as well.

According to recent reports, honestly, it is well past time The Game Awards introduced a dedicated Best Remake/Remaster category, as in my experience, these projects are often judged unfairly by the jury when stacked directly against brand-newly introduced releases. Without diving too deep into that debate, if Dragon Quest VII Reimagined had been a brand-new original title rather than a remake, I am almost certain it would have landed a TGA nomination, particularly in Best RPG.

It has been revealed that dragon Quest VII Reimagined was, well, thoughtfully reimagined for modern audiences. The original release was notoriously bloated, taking hours just to reach your very first combat encounter. While the remake trimmed away a few islands from the classic version, those cuts worked wonders for the pacing. Both combat and character progression were cleanly streamlined, and random encounters were ditched in favor of visible monsters roaming the map. Dragon Quest VII Reimagined is a phenomenal achievement that delights newcomers and longtime veterans alike.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it debuted on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was revealed back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly revealed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it rolled out, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating presently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

Once you’re past the initial hump, you’ll probably be looking for where to find things like mushrooms, bugs, fish, and birds, so definitely bookmark those, too. If you simply like free stuff, our Heartopia codes page is a must read before playing.

A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that light can carry vast amounts of information, but developing faster and more efficient optical communication systems requires precise control over how it travels.
  • A research team led by KAIST has uncovered detailed information about how light moves through BTO and how much of it the material absorbs.
  • KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) unveiled the results on November 8.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that light can carry vast amounts of information, but developing faster and more efficient optical communication systems requires precise control over how it travels. Scientists have now made an important advance in understanding barium titanate (BTO), a promising material that could help improve the performance of future devices that transmit information using light.

A research team led by KAIST has uncovered detailed information about how light moves through BTO and how much of it the material absorbs. These properties have been difficult to measure accurately for decades because of the crystal's complicated internal structure. The new findings provide engineers with a more reliable foundation for designing optical devices that minimize signal loss and support faster data transmission.

KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) unveiled the results on November 8. The research was led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, working with Professor Harry A. Atwater's group at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co. Together, the researchers examined how BTO interacts with light across wavelengths extending from the ultraviolet to the far-infrared.

Why Barium Titanate Could Transform Optical Communications.

One of BTO's most valuable characteristics is its ability to change how it affects light when electricity is applied. This behavior, called the Pockels effect, gives the material a strong electro-optic response and makes it especially attractive for optical modulators. These components convert electrical information into signals carried by light, making them key building blocks for advanced communication systems.

In a recent development, however, producing reliable devices requires a detailed understanding of two fundamental optical properties. The refractive index describes how light travels through a material, while the extinction coefficient indicates how strongly the material absorbs it. Engineers need both measurements to predict how light will behave inside a waveguide, a structure designed to direct light along a specific path, and how much of the optical signal may be lost.

Getting consistent measurements from BTO has been surprisingly challenging. The material can contain multiple microscopic regions, called domains, in which the crystal structure points in different directions. Because these regions interact with light differently, measurements of an entire sample can combine several distinct responses. This has contributed to widely conflicting reports of BTO's optical properties over many decades.

Solving a Decades-Old Mystery About Light.

Sources indicate that to overcome this problem, the researchers used a sophisticated measurement method known as Mueller matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry. The technique examines how the polarization of light changes when light reflects from or passes through a material, allowing scientists to investigate its optical behavior in detail.

In a recent development, rather than relying on crystals containing a complicated mixture of differently oriented regions, the team studied two types of single-crystal samples with relatively consistent domain orientations. This approach helped minimize overlapping optical responses and allowed the researchers to identify the material's underlying properties more accurately.

Their measurements spanned wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), covering an exceptionally broad range of light from ultraviolet to far-infrared. Since a material's optical behavior changes with wavelength, the scientists divided the spectrum into three regions and applied a different analytical approach to each. This revealed how BTO's refractive index and light absorption depend on both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The researchers also investigated a particularly key range in which BTO allows nearly all incoming light to pass through. By combining ellipsometry with separate measurements of light transmission, they detected extremely low absorption, determining extinction coefficients of approximately 10-5 in the 2-10 μm wavelength range. These precise values will help engineers estimate how much light is lost as it travels through or remains confined within optical components.

According to recent reports, in another advance, the team developed a way to predict the combined optical behavior of crystals containing multiple domains. Their method uses the orientations of those domains and the proportion of the crystal occupied by each to calculate the material's overall response to light.

Opening the Door to Faster Data Transmission and Quantum Technology.

The results could make the development of future optical devices more predictable and efficient. With accurate information about BTO's behavior, engineers can model how light will travel through components of different shapes and dimensions before manufacturing them. They can also better estimate absorption losses, potentially reducing the need for repeated prototypes, costly redesigns, and extensive testing.

The potential benefits extend beyond conventional optical communications. BTO could also play an important role in devices that produce light at different wavelengths, as well as photonic circuits that use light to process quantum information. Such technologies depend on controlling light with exceptional precision.

"This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light," remarked Professor Min Seok Jang.

Jang also emphasized that the findings could contribute to optical communication devices capable of transmitting data faster while reducing light loss. The improved understanding of BTO may also support the development of quantum photonic technologies, where precise manipulation of light is essential.

Recent findings suggest that the study was published online on October 20, 2026, in ACS Photonics. Jiwon Kang, a Ph.D. candidate in KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, and Dr. Nina Hong of J.A. Woollam Co. served as co-first authors. Professors Min Seok Jang of KAIST and Harry A. Atwater of Caltech were the corresponding authors.

Sources indicate that funding was provided through the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program administered by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with support from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program administered by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with support from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1053 w)

Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field.
  • It has been revealed that an international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss.
  • Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

It has been revealed that an international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago.

The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered fresh genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who revealed similar symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that the study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

According to recent reports, at first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," mentioned Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a upcoming variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.".

How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision.

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

According to recent reports, unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

According to recent reports, however, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

It has been revealed that "We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan mentioned. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.".

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss.

An vital question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Recent findings suggest that researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

It has been revealed that beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.".

Sources indicate that by revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

Recent findings suggest that the study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, as discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content.
  • The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the upcoming maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it intends to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

According to recent reports, as discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a massive component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the upcoming maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

According to recent reports, another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

It has been revealed that more Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios mentioned we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

Sources indicate that for context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its challenges elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on promptly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer.
  • According to recent reports, seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marvel Cosmic Invasion was a bit of a dream game for me; I loved the X-Men arcade game in the '90s, so when Tribute Games released the excellent Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge in 2022, I immediately hoped they'd revitalize other licensed brawler franchises released by Konami in the late '80s and early '90s. While we still haven't heard any word of a latest brawler starring The Simpsons, Tribute did follow up its Turtle triumph with Marvel Cosmic Invasion, another throwback side-scrolling beat 'em up, this time starring Marvel's mightiest.

According to recent reports, I played through Marvel Cosmic Invasion multiple times and had a blast, but I moved on promptly, as I didn't feel the need to collect different palette-swaps of the many heroes on offer. Even after Cyclops and The Thing joined the roster as DLC in May, I still saw Cosmic Invasion as a game in the rearview. That changes this week, as The Siege of Castle Doom not only adds two additional playable characters (Invisible Woman and Doctor Doom), but also a mode that has the potential to bring me back for more runs for the foreseeable future.

According to recent reports, seeing that Annihilus is threatening the universe, Doom decides to take matters into his own hands. Unfortunately, much in the way that it seems that he may try to fix the multiversal incursions in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, Victor Von Doom's solution in Marvel Cosmic Invasion – the Cosmic Inductor – would lead to untold death and destruction. In The Siege of Castle Doom, you select your team and fight your way through various floors of the stronghold belonging to the man who is perhaps Marvel's greatest villain. Your goal is to fight through the winding, randomized hallways of Castle Doomstadt, charging Reed Richards' Stabilizer and tactically bolstering your team along the way, before Doctor Doom can enact his plan.

Industry observers note that as for the new playable characters, Doctor Doom is less agile, but his attacks pack a whallop, while Invisible Woman's force fields and speed make her the more versatile pick. I don't know that I see either of them replacing my mains from the base game, but I had fun experimenting with them throughout this mode. Regardless of which character you choose from the expanding roster, you still must traverse Castle Doomstadt before Doom achieves his objective.

Industry observers note that fighting through waves of enemies across differently themed and booby-trapped rooms, you encounter all manner of foes from the base game, as well as new minion types from Doom. When you defeat enemies, they drop batteries that charge your Stabilizer, letting you even the odds and stop Doom. Conversely, each time an enemy hits your character, it charges Doom's Cosmic Inductor, inching him closer to victory and making his minions faster and stronger in the process. As you might expect, the rooms get harder the deeper you go, and while each player starts with two characters to swap between, if a character completely depletes their health, they're gone for good, making it even tougher. As such, you need to keep your eyes on each character's health and swap them out when it makes sense.

Industry observers note that as you complete each room, you can choose which path to take to augment your characters with new special abilities. True to the roguelite structure, as you complete rooms, you can also buff your characters' stats within the run. Certain rooms offer extra batteries to help your Stabilizer charge, while others offer new and upgraded equipment. There's also one that promises random events that can easily alter the trajectory of your run for better or worse. Though I often enjoyed boosting attack stats to make enemies less like damage sponges, I had to balance that against buffing their health to keep them alive and charging the Stabilizer to have a fighting chance.

Industry observers note that beyond the in-run upgrades and modifiers, you can also amp up the action run-over-run through upgrades in Reed's Lab, which add to the pool of modifiers you can select from at the start of each run. The expansion also adds upcoming palettes for existing heroes, plus new music by composer Tee Lopes. While I've only done a few runs of The Siege of Castle Doom (each taking between 45 and 90 minutes, depending on how successful you are), I feel a revitalized sense of excitement for Marvel Cosmic Invasion. Tribute claims completionists can spend upwards of 15 hours in this new mode, which has me champing at the bit to dive back into what will likely be my primary way of interacting with Marvel Cosmic Invasion going forward.

Marvel Cosmic Invasion – The Siege of Castle Doom is available today on all platforms, and it is a strong addition to an already great game. You can read our review of the base version of Marvel Cosmic Invasion here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension.
  • Sources indicate that losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile.
  • According to recent reports, the findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Sources indicate that losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a newly introduced study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

According to recent reports, the findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

In a recent development, the research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," says Cohen. "The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.".

AI Analysis Reveals New Benefits of Brown Fat.

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

Recent findings suggest that the team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover crucial details about brown fat and its effects on health.

It has been revealed that nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

Sources indicate that the analysis demonstrated that brown fat's location could be just as crucial as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

"For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he indicates. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers.".

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat.

It has been revealed that as the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

It has been revealed that to explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

Recent findings suggest that even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

Recent findings suggest that "The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," says Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.".

According to recent reports, additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan demonstrated increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health.

Beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric complications," states Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

It has been revealed that however, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

The discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

Losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

Recent findings suggest that "There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start.".

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1658 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 10 Hard to Beat Sega Genesis JRPGs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while many of us played our first JRPGs on PS1 or PS2, they existed way before then.
  • There's a good mix even with these JRPG adventures, which feature sword and sorcery fantasy, far flung future and others besides.
  • As for how they're ranked, we dug deep to find critical reception, and did our best to sort these JRPGs accordingly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while many of us played our first JRPGs on PS1 or PS2, they existed way before then. The catch was, many of the JRPGs on older systems were incredibly experimental games. They were less clearly defined, but still worthwhile. That especially applies for the Sega Genesis, which featured many hard to beat JRPGs.

There's a good mix even with these JRPG adventures, which feature sword and sorcery fantasy, far flung future and others besides. No matter what, though, they all featured some capacity to upgrade your characters, and many were turn-based as well.

As for how they're ranked, we dug deep to find critical reception, and did our best to sort these JRPGs accordingly. So join me in my time machine as we head back to the glory days of the Sega Genesis with these hard to beat JRPGs!

While the Dungeons & Dragons series has come a long way, it's fascinating to see where it started, at least in videogames. And though Dungeons & Dragons: Warriors of the Eternal Sun was mechanically a pretty weird JRPG, it featured a pretty engaging plot.

In a recent development, it starts with typical warfare against lowly goblins, then has the human army warped to a mysterious land of the Eternal Sun. Meanwhile, something called the Burrower is driving all your allies insane. It's surprisingly Lovecraftian, and quite neat, especially from back in the Sega Genesis era.

According to recent reports, this JRPG has a lot of understandable dungeon crawler energy, with players mustering a party of four different characters whose race and class determines everything. And like any good JRPG, as you level up, you'll learn powerful upcoming skills, though much is decided by the RNG roll of a dice.

Even though I'm not a huge fan of the whole Mystery Dungeon craze, I can see the general appeal. I discovered them with the Pokemon offshoots, but they started way sooner. One of the first examples is simply called Fatal Labyrinth.

It's about chasing a vicious dragon that guards a Holy Goblet, and safely navigating 30 floors of dangers to get there. Enemies don't move or act until you do, so there's inherent strategy in Fatal Labyrinth. More unique, you'll do well to discover whether scrolls and potions hurt or harm you, and using them accordingly.

Perhaps the most charmingly old school aspect of the game is that gold only serves one purpose – blinging out your funeral when you die! So make sure to stock up on vital food and powerful gear, and maybe your journey won't have an ignominious end.

According to recent reports, in a way, The Immortal makes a better novel than a videogame. It's the tale of a call from deep within a labyrinth from the wizard Mordamir. You're not the person he called, named Dunric, but you'll do! Along the way, you'll navigate through several levels, ride magic carpets, and discover the true nightmare of what happened.

It has been revealed that like any good JRPG, there's NPCs here, and you can even cast magic spells to roast your enemies. Those include the likes of goblins, flesh-eating slimes, shades and even a diabolical dragon. Also surprising for the era, The Immortal was surprisingly graphic and violent at times.

While the game features lots of fun fantasy elements, it's also painfully linear, which made some feel it didn't do enough for the genre. Still, a good early attempt, and one that experimented in some meaningful ways.

In a recent development, I think it's fair to say that The Lord of the Rings inspired Sword of Vermilion on the Sega Genesis. The game features King Tsarkon, who is warped by a magical ring, and twisted to evil ends. A valiant knight named Blade saves the good king's child, and then 18 years later, counsels the prince on his deathbed. It's up to him to honor his dead father and his valiant protector.

Sources indicate that as for how Sword of Vermilion actually plays, it has a lot of ARPG mechanics. Furthermore, the gameplay shifts depending on a variety of circumstances, and alternates between top down and side views for the exploration and boss battles.

It has been revealed that while the game has a lot of fun arcade energy, the graphics weren't seen as a high point, even back when it first released. On the plus side, it was also a console exclusive, meaning only those who owned a Sega Genesis experienced this classic JRPG.

In a recent development, I'm usually a fan of when developers try something fresh. But with Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom, it was actually a brand new team brought in who hadn't worked on the previous two games. On the plus side, they tried new features like branching narrative paths and multiple endings. On the negative, in some ways this didn't feel like a Phantasy Star adventure.

Industry observers note that phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom actually spans multiple generations, meaning you'll play as the descendants of your starting main character, which honestly feels a bit like Fire Emblem. Depending on who you marry, you'll continue the game with different abilities as various children.

This adventure downplays the Technique system, but it makes up for it with auto-battle and an icon-based menu. Either way, this is traditional turn-based fare that, at least for me, makes me feel right at home in any JRPG adventure.

Unlike the last game, Ys III: Wanderers From Ys is very much a direct follow up to the previous Ys adventures. It features Adol Christin, mysterious statues and the advent of a brutal demon named Galbalan. The game also handles stats, equipment and experience the same as the other games.

According to recent reports, where Ys III: Wanderers From Ys stands apart is that it utilizes a side-scrolling view instead of the more traditional top-down style. Also, you can't just auto attack anymore, and instead need to pres a button to have Adol swing his blade or cast spells.

Sources indicate that while the game can be a bit grindy and repetitive, those who were already fans of the Ys series were very happy with this adventure. It could have done more to branch out, perhaps, but sometimes if it's not broken, you don't need to fix anything.

Whenever you hear that Treasure developed a game, you have to pay attention. They make some of the most creative games out there, though usually it's more platformers than JRPGs. In fairness, Light Crusader is a bit of an odd duck, combining the JRPG genre with isometric graphics and action adventure mechanics.

Sources indicate that you play Sir David, who is trying to save the kidnapped citizens of Green Row. He can run and jump, swing his blade and generally beat up monsters. But he's also capable of casting elemental magic. They can be cast individually or combined, buffing David or healing him, amongst other uses.

Industry observers note that along the way, you'll discover the entire game is about the slighted advances of a diabolical wizard. He wanted desperately to marry the Queen of Green Row, and in his petulance, eventually summons a demon. Definitely a quirky adventure, but a memorable one, even years and years later.

It took me a long while to get to Langrisser, a tactical series as popular in some spheres as Fire Emblem or Tactics Ogre. It didn't start with that name, though. Originally, it was called Warsong, and it was a pretty substantial deal on the Sega Genesis. It's a fun but pretty brutal tactical JRPG adventure.

Sources indicate that like many brutal games, Warsong features permadeath, meaning if you're not careful, you could lose some of your best characters forever. Your commanders determine what units you can bring into battle, such as powerful Griffons.

Sources indicate that ultimately, careful strategy rewards you with powerful upgrades to your commanders, including changing their classes. If all that wasn't enough, Warsong also features great music composed by Noriyuki Iwadare. A great game if you're strong enough to get through it relatively unscathed.

According to recent reports, there aren't all that many times I get really jealous about console exclusivity these days. But one of those classics I wish I had played back in the day was Shining Force II. It wasn't just good, but it was considered one of the best tactical JRPGs of all time.

Some of the reasons people felt that way was due to how open-ended the game was, as well as the great visual flair. It alternated between top-down while exploring, and side scrolling during combat. Either way, the game was challenging, and forced you to lead Bowie and friends carefully.

As for the plot, Shining Force II takes place 55 years after Shining Force Gaiden: Final Conflict, and is about Zeon's mayhem. But even if you didn't play the previous games, this is one tactical adventure that holds up, though it's also far from an easy time.

One of the more iconic games I played back in the day was Alundra. It was sort of like Zelda, but not really, and it really captivated me. One game that came before it was called Landstalker, a game about a treasure hunter named Nigel.

While Landstalker may not seem like a JRPG at first, there are a couple of reasons it qualifies as one. Even though you don't level up by traditional means, you can take on sidequests to improve your stats. There's also ways to improve your health, and even equip more powerful gear. A lot of it just requires a desire to explore as much as possible.

Industry observers note that much of the game's overall challenge comes from devious death traps and gnarly puzzles, not to mention challenging boss battles. Definitely a strange old-school JRPG, but one that managed to delight fans by taking plenty of creative risks.

For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, how often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout.
  • Industry observers note that the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues.
  • It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, how often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly crucial for supporting mental well-being.

Industry observers note that the research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health.

It has been revealed that depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to new academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an important research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

According to recent reports, to investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

According to recent reports, at the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity.

In a recent development, the researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise revealed the same relationship with mental health.

According to recent reports, exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week highlighted a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health.

Taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

Recent findings suggest that however, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life.".

"Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an important part of a healthy learning environment.".

Funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fnatic has confirmed the departure of its longest-serving player, jungler Razork, who is set to join Team Heretics. With support Lospa also set to leave, the London club faces a near-total LEC roster rebuild for 2027.

Fnatic has made its first confirmed exit official as it rebuilds its LEC roster for 2027. Razork was the London club’s longest-serving player and its main playmaker. He leaves after five seasons in the jungle.

In a recent development, the club marked the departure with a farewell video titled “Thank You, Iván”. In it, Fnatic recalls him arriving as a young player with huge ambition. He had entered the LEC with Misfits Gaming in 2020 before moving to Fnatic in 2022. The club later extended his contract to run through 2026.

His next stop appears to be Team Heretics. Sheep Esports reported that the 26-year-old will play alongside midlaner Jackies and support Jun. Heretics had already tried to sign him a year earlier. On that occasion it agreed a buyout with Fnatic but could not agree terms with the player.

It has been revealed that the rebuild runs deeper than the jungle. Every Fnatic team member except Lospa was due out of contract in 2026. The support was signed until the end of 2027.

That deal will not keep him at Fnatic either. Lospa has reportedly agreed verbally to join SK Gaming for 2027. No buyout is involved in moving his contract between the two clubs. With that move, the one contract running beyond 2026 also leaves the club.

In the jungle, Yike is set to replace Razork in a 2027 line-up of Soboro, Yike, Vladi, Doggo and Labrov, according to Sheep Esports sources.

Industry observers note that the overhaul follows a difficult year. Fnatic finished eighth in LEC 2026 Versus. It then placed seventh in Spring, which ended on 10 May. Summer brought the same finishing position.

A loss to GIANTX on 30 August kept the team out of the Summer playoffs. That defeat left the club absent from Worlds for the first time since 2016.

Industry observers note that for the UK scene, the scale of change matters. Fnatic is one of the LEC’s best-supported clubs among British fans.

The club has also opened a search for a League of Legends General Manager. Its job advert claims Fnatic goes into a rebuild in 2027. The new hire will run recruitment of players, coaches and staff, including transfers and benchings, and will manage the team’s budget.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The blueprint is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content upgrade each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one fresh map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

Sources indicate that while we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

In a recent development, january’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a upcoming clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating.
  • The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes.
  • "We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," notes Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a upcoming clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," notes Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have notable therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone.".

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets.

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss.

It has been revealed that participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating aims, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

It has been revealed that researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

According to recent reports, by the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

Keto Diet Reduces Liver Fat by 67%.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several notable indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

It has been revealed that the ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

Recent findings suggest that one result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," states Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes.

According to recent reports, the benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

According to recent reports, these differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially vital distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

Industry observers note that "GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen indicates. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits.".

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an key role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

  • Listening to the inner truths of the game’s various NPCs can get a bit wild, but these are the most unhinged and strange thoughts to be found in Hyrule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you’ve spent time wandering around Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, and you decided to pay the Happy Mask Salesman a visit. He gave you a few masks, you made a few sales, and you have received the Mask of Truth in return.

Industry observers note that what does this mask do? Well, it reveals the inner thoughts of the game’s various NPCs. I am not sure if you have paid attention to Nintendo games recently, but they have been adding in some interesting NPC dialogue.

Listening to the inner truths of the game’s various NPCs can get a bit wild, but these are the most unhinged and strange thoughts to be found in Hyrule.

If you walk around the town square in Castle Town, you can find some rather colorful NPCs, but one of the most unassuming of them is the old woman who stares at the fountain. She seems so sweet, but she is actually a thief.

Listening to her inner thoughts, you see that they say, “The quality of the items people are losing has really gone downhill recently… Is that a recession indicator?”.

This hits a little close to home considering many have questioned if the U.S. is entering a recession. Along with this, it is obvious that she is taking some of the goods that people have lost and keeping them for herself.

If you continue your search around the fountain in Castle Town, you can find a young couple who are dancing. While they seem rather sweet, their inner thoughts tell a completely different story.

Industry observers note that when you read the thoughts of the woman, it will say that she hopes that the man doesn’t break her heart. It is a sad thought to be had because she is clearly worried about her future.

When you read the man’s thoughts, you see they say, “Wait… What was this one’s name again?” Clearly, this isn’t his only crush, and he is stringing this poor woman along so he has someone to dance with. Yes… dance with.

Industry observers note that some of the guards around Castle Town aren’t very excited about their job. In fact, some of them find it boring doing patrols all the time. One guard in particular thinks about it pretty frequently.

In a recent development, when interacting with the guard in the room with the pots, his inner truth will say, “Guards… Soldiers… Heroes… It’s their fault there’s so much peace around here. Hm… What if I…”.

Sources indicate that the thought trails off after that, but you can clearly tell what he is thinking about. The man wants some chaos, and he is clearing thinking about being the cause of mentioned chaos if something doesn’t happen soon.

It has been revealed that you may have seen the bearded man wandering around Castle Town in the past and Kakariko Village in the future. His beard is magnificent, and he will definitely tell you about it. However, he is secretly questioning its cleanliness.

When you listen to his inner thoughts, they say, “I wonder if it’s true that beards are about as dirty as toilets…” For someone with such a massive beard, he shouldn’t be thinking that he is dirty, unless he wants to shave it off.

This is a massive contrast to what he will tell you when you speak to him, as he will typically say that he has a fantastic beard, and will even offer to locate Ganondorf.

Shiro is one of the many NPCs you can find around Kakariko Village, and you also help him out by rescuing him from the Gerudo as an adult. Well, he isn’t the happiest carpenter around. In fact, he is rather depressed.

Recent findings suggest that his inner thoughts read, “How does one escape their own dreary life? ‘Cause I can’t do this forever.” Granted, he didn’t seem the happiest when I rescued him from the Gerudo, but I never would have guessed that he was this depressed.

Looking into his thoughts, he seems like he could use some therapy because it sounds like he has been hanging around Lumiose City in Pokémon Legends: Z-A for too long.

There’s a pair of laughing men who appear in Castle Town and Kakariko. No matter what is happening, the pair consistently laugh at one another. They typically talk about stories they find funny, with the one laughing at the other for getting caught sneaking into the castle or falling off a horse.

However, when you read their inner thoughts, the one claims, “It’s exhausting wearing this forced smile all the time.” The other one will remark about how he knows his friend’s smile is fake.

It’s sad that they continue to laugh constantly. Maybe they should just try to chill out for once and give up on the laughter. Are they cursed? Maybe they are cursed.

If you have explored Kakariko Village, you are for sure aware of the cucco lady. All of her cuccos get out of the pen, and you must go rescue them for a reward. In the future, she is living with a questionable character.

Recent findings suggest that if you use the Mask of Truth while you are an adult, you will catch her inner thoughts. They say, “That guy who lives with me always makes the most intense eye contact. He must really love cuccos…”.

Sources indicate that what she is describing does not sound healthy at all. In fact, it sounds almost like something bad is going to happen and she is just waiting for the inevitable. Maybe she should choose a different place to live or kick the guy out.

Recent findings suggest that there is an old man who likes to wander around Castle Town. He will go in and out of shops, but mostly he will walk around the fountain. Just be careful listening to his thoughts because he has a particular woman on his mind.

His inner thoughts read, “This kid… The mask’s neat and all, but I’m more interested in finding a particular damsel…” While it doesn’t seem so bad at first, if you talk to him, you can piece things together.

Talking to him, he will make remarks about how he is looking for a lady who can make a potion, and will gawk at how beautiful she is. He will also casually talk about how we are at the age to be thinking about that.
